---
title: "Guarantees and limits"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
vignette: >
  %\VignetteIndexEntry{Guarantees and limits}
  %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown}
  %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8}
---


A passed in-memory trial establishes that its retained input passed the declared
contract and configured checks. Without a contract, the result is `unvalidated`:
retained data can be collected for exploration, but the write gate refuses
publication. A schema inferred from the same data is descriptive, not independent
validation. Existing scripts that publish contract-free products must add explicit
contracts before publication.

A trial does not reserve a future source version, check target permissions or
capacity, or rule out publication conflicts. A later run can see different
external data. Within generic lazy execution, quality checks and the writer use
the same materialized candidate. Definition construction does not read or write
sources. Execution can do both.

Recognized random and time-dependent quality predicates require an explicit
volatility declaration. Volatile evidence is not reproducible approval or reusable
cache evidence. Static analysis detects known calls; it cannot prove determinism
of arbitrary closures, hidden dependencies or external services. Two identical
evaluations would not establish that proof either.

Lake releases preserve published versions during ordinary publication. Publication
coordinates registry state and storage, but a process crash can leave intermediate
objects. Inspect interrupted runs and use the lake recovery and cleanup functions
before retrying. Do not assume an external target adapter provides the same
transaction or recovery guarantees as a managed lake.

Local lake writes require one coordinated writer. Do not run independent local
writers against the same catalog. Shared writers require the supported PostgreSQL
coordination configuration; using an object store alone does not provide locking.
The PostgreSQL integration job exercises separate writer processes. Backend and
crash behavior still require testing against the deployment configuration.

Writer bookkeeping is process-local and keyed to the connection configuration.
A future or targets worker must open its own resources and close those it owns.
Do not serialize live database connections into workers. Definitions are ordinary
R values; closures supplied by users can themselves capture mutable state.

“Immutable” describes normal release publication, not a legal retention policy or
undeletable storage. Operators must define retention for data, registry metadata,
quality evidence, frozen reports, backups and downstream catalogs. Deleting one
release does not erase its copies. Resolve deletion requests across those stores;
DataRaft does not provide a universal subject-erasure operation.

Use `dr_verify_releases(lake, release_ids = NULL)` to compare stored releases
with their recorded row counts and content fingerprints. Row ordering does not
affect the fingerprint. Older releases migrated without an original fingerprint
are explicitly `unverified`; migration cannot retroactively prove their history.
Verification scans selected data and keeps one digest per row in memory. The
fingerprint uses the DBI representation and is not guaranteed portable across R
or driver serialization changes.

This detects accidental mutation relative to the registry. An administrator able
to change both data and registry can also change the recorded fingerprint. It is
not an independent authenticity proof. Direct database clients must be quiescent
during verification; library coordination cannot constrain arbitrary SQL clients.
